findings.source_passage: seeking increase of wretchedness in every reflection that could afford it
findings.source_locator: paragraph on Elinor/Marianne grief, near end of source
findings.why_it_matters: This clause is distinctively Austenian in its ironic precision — 'seeking increase of wretchedness' is a textually distinctive phrase that captures the novel's central thematic critique of performed sensibility; its excision flattens the satirical register of the passage.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'seeking increase of wretchedness in every reflection that could afford it' within the grief paragraph rather than condensing to 'and resolved against ever admitting consolation.'

findings.source_passage: he was very young when he married, and very fond of his wife
findings.why_it_matters: This clause carries quiet ironic weight — the explanation for why he 'might have been made amiable' is the contrast between youthful affection and the wife he actually got; its omission weakens the satirical logic of the characterisation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'for he was very young when he married, and very fond of his wife' before the pivot to Mrs. John Dashwood as caricature.

findings.source_passage: so earnestly did she despise her daughter-in-law for it
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'So acutely did Mrs. Dashwood feel'
findings.why_it_matters: The word 'despise' is a sharp register marker; the draft softens this to mere feeling the 'ungracious behaviour,' losing the intensity of Mrs. Dashwood's reaction that Austen underscores with the doubled construction.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'so earnestly did she despise her daughter-in-law for it' to preserve the full rhetorical parallel and tonal force.

summary: The draft is largely faithful and preserves all major signatures verbatim or near-verbatim, with only minor voice-flattening in the grief passage (loss of 'seeking increase of wretchedness') and two small excisions that trim Austen's ironic precision without rising to high severity.
